card.chief_complaint: dark urine and acute kidney injury

ask.changes_what: A positive exposure history should lead to stopping or dose-adjusting the agent, avoiding further nephrotoxins and monitoring creatinine; still assess obstruction and volume status.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute AKI solely to a drug or contrast when there is oliguria, sepsis, hypotension or possible obstruction; these still need evaluation.
ask.escalation_warning: AKI with hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uremic symptoms needs urgent nephrology review regardless of the exposure history.
ask.how: Reconcile all drugs against the chart and pharmacy record, including over-the-counter NSAIDs and herbal products: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, aminoglycosides, vancomycin (with piperacillin-tazobactam), PPIs, and any iodinated contrast. For each, record start date, dose change and timing relative to the creatinine rise.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure lowers the likelihood of drug-related AKI and contrast nephropathy, redirecting attention to hypovolemia, sepsis, obstruction and intrinsic renal disease.
ask.pitfalls: Patients under-report OTC NSAIDs; PPI-associated AIN can begin weeks to months after the start; contrast-associated AKI is often confounded by the illness that prompted imaging, so timing alone does not prove causation.
ask.positive_finding: A nephrotoxin started or dosed within days of the creatinine rise, or contrast within 48-72 h, makes drug-induced AKI (hemodynamic, ATN or AIN) a leading candidate and identifies an immediately reversible factor.
ask.prerequisites: Access to medication administration and imaging records; collateral history for patients who cannot report OTC use.
ask.title: Nephrotoxin and contrast exposure history (NSAID, ACEi/ARB, diuretic, aminoglycoside, vancomycin, PPI, iodinated contrast; timing)

ask.changes_what: Positive: hold/adjust the culprit, check orthostatic vitals, ECG, creatinine and electrolytes; negative: pursue arrhythmic, structural, vasovagal or infectious causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not accept a medication explanation as final in patients with exertional syncope, syncope while supine, palpitations preceding syncope, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
ask.escalation_warning: Bradycardia or high-grade AV block, QT prolongation, symptomatic hypotension with AKI, or opioid/sedative toxicity with reduced consciousness need monitored care and antidote/withdrawal decisions.
ask.how: Reconcile every drug (prescribed, OTC, herbal, recreational) against the pharmacy list: antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, PDE5 inhibitors, rate-slowing agents (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCB, digoxin), QT-prolonging drugs, sedatives/opioids, psychotropics, insulin/sulfonylureas, NSAIDs/ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i. Note start dates, dose changes and timing of the last dose versus the event.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug or no temporal relationship lowers the probability of medication effect but does not exclude intrinsic cardiac or neurological causes.
ask.pitfalls: Patients omit over-the-counter, recreational and 'as needed' drugs; drug effects are amplified by age, renal impairment, volume depletion and drug-drug interactions, so a long-standing drug can still be the cause after a change elsewhere. Attributing syncope to drugs without ECG review can miss conduction disease unmasked by the drug.
ask.positive_finding: A new or up-titrated vasoactive, rate-slowing, sedative or diuretic drug (or an intercurrent illness reducing intake/clearance) temporally linked to the event supports drug-induced orthostatic hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, hypovolemia/AKI or delirium.
ask.prerequisites: Access to an accurate medication list (pharmacy fill data, carer, containers); ask specifically about new drugs and dose escalations within the past 2-4 weeks.
ask.title: Antihypertensive / sedative / new-medication review (timing of last doses)

ask.changes_what: Positive → CK, creatinine, potassium, urinalysis; start IV fluids; assess compartments. Negative → still send CK if found down, post-seizure or toxin-exposed.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not exclude rhabdomyolysis by history in obtunded, intoxicated or found-down patients — send CK.
ask.escalation_warning: Tense painful compartment, hyperkalemia or rising creatinine → urgent surgical and nephrology involvement.
ask.how: Ask about muscle pain, weakness, swelling and dark tea/cola-coloured urine, and exposures: found down/prolonged immobilization, seizure, extreme exertion or heat, crush or trauma, cocaine/amphetamines, alcohol, statins/fibrates, antipsychotics (NMS), recent infection. Palpate for tender, swollen or tense muscle compartments and check distal pulses and sensation.
ask.negative_finding: Absent muscle symptoms or dark urine do not exclude rhabdomyolysis; many cases are oligosymptomatic and even qualitative urine myoglobin was positive in only 19% of 475 inpatients (PMID 16267412, Abstract). Measure CK whenever risk factors exist.
ask.pitfalls: Dark urine also comes from hematuria, hemoglobinuria or bilirubin. In 60% of cases multiple causes co-exist and toxins account for 46% (PMID 16267412, Abstract); CK peaks at 24–72 h, so an early value may be modest (unverified recall).
ask.positive_finding: Myalgia or weakness with dark urine after immobilization, exertion, seizure or toxin exposure strongly suggests rhabdomyolysis; check CK and a urine dipstick (heme-positive without red cells).
ask.prerequisites: Collateral history for obtunded or intoxicated patients; medication and drug-use review.
ask.title: Muscle pain/weakness, prolonged immobilization or exertion, dark cola-colored urine

ask.changes_what: Positive: stop the suspect drug, check urinalysis for pyuria/WBC casts and consider biopsy/steroids early; negative should not remove AIN from the differential of unexplained AKI on a new drug.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of fever/rash/arthralgia to exclude AIN, especially with PPIs or NSAIDs; do not attribute fever plus AKI to AIN without considering sepsis.
ask.escalation_warning: Rapidly rising creatinine, oliguria, or hyperkalemia on a suspect drug needs same-day nephrology review; biopsy decisions are time-sensitive because delayed drug withdrawal worsens recovery.
ask.how: Take a dated medication history for the preceding weeks to months (antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors) and ask about fever, new rash, joint pains, and flank pain since starting; inspect the skin. Correlate the time course with the onset of creatinine rise.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of the triad is the rule: in biopsy series each feature is present in fewer than half of cases and the full triad in roughly 10%, so absence does not lower the probability of AIN meaningfully.
ask.pitfalls: PPI- and NSAID-induced AIN are typically oligosymptomatic with long latency; fever and rash after a new drug also occur with drug fever, DRESS, and infection without AIN. Definitive diagnosis requires kidney biopsy.
ask.positive_finding: Fever, rash, or arthralgia emerging after a new drug in a patient with unexplained AKI (often with sterile pyuria) supports drug-induced AIN and should prompt stopping the drug and nephrology input.
ask.prerequisites: Complete drug list including over-the-counter and recently stopped agents.
ask.title: Rash, fever, arthralgia after new drug (AIN triad)

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant hypovolemia/bleeding or medication-related OH and act; negative: large blood loss unlikely, but moderate loss still possible.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is frankly hypotensive, has an unstable spine/pelvis, or cannot safely bear weight.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing measurements in a patient who is already hypotensive, too dizzy or weak to stand safely, or has an unstable spine or pelvis; a patient too dizzy to stand counts as a positive test.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive test in a patient with possible bleeding indicates large volume loss and should trigger resuscitation and source search, not observation.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.target_condition: Large acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.target_condition: Moderate acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy
evidence.quote: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent, even after up to 1150 mL of blood loss (sensitivity, 33%; 95% CI, 21%-47%, for supine hypotension)
evidence.target_condition: Blood loss up to 1150 mL - supine hypotension (comparator finding, not postural)

examine.how: Measure BP and pulse after >=2 min supine, then have the patient stand and repeat at 1 and 3 min (standing, not sitting). Record SBP fall >=20 or DBP fall >=10 mmHg, pulse rise >=30/min, and whether the patient is too dizzy to stand (count that as positive).
examine.negative_finding: A normal postural pulse response argues strongly against large blood loss (LR- about 0.03) but misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%). Normal orthostatics do not exclude hypovolemia from vomiting/diarrhea.
examine.pitfalls: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent even after 1 L blood loss. Beta-blockers blunt the pulse response; sitting instead of standing lowers sensitivity; mild postural dizziness alone has no proven value.
examine.positive_finding: A postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness is highly specific (98%) for blood loss and is nearly always present after large (>1 L) hemorrhage. In an older patient with syncope, an SBP fall >=20 mmHg reproducing symptoms supports orthostatic hypotension, though asymptomatic falls are common with age and medications.
examine.prerequisites: Automated or manual cuff, an assistant to steady the patient, supine rest of at least 2 minutes first.
examine.title: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing

examine.changes_what: Prolonged CRT in shock: treat as ongoing hypoperfusion and reassess after resuscitation; normal CRT does not rule out hypovolemia.
examine.contraindications: Not interpretable on a cold, cyanotic or vasoconstricted limb, with peripheral arterial disease, or in the presence of nail polish/false nails.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use CRT to exclude hypovolemia or bleeding in adults; do not interpret on cold, vasoconstricted or peripherally diseased limbs.
examine.escalation_warning: Persistently prolonged CRT after initial resuscitation in septic shock marks a high-mortality group and should prompt reassessment of perfusion and escalation, not reassurance.

evidence.quote: 26% for the orthostatic group, and 46% for the hypotensive group
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical hypovolemia group assignment (hypotension); age-sex specific CRT upper limit of normal
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (ED patients with suggestive history and frank hypotension)

evidence.population: 19 adult ED patients with history suggestive of hypovolemia and abnormal orthostatic vital signs

evidence.reference_standard: Clinical hypovolemia group assignment (abnormal orthostatics); age-sex specific CRT upper limit of normal
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (ED patients with suggestive history and abnormal orthostatic vital signs)

evidence.citation: Ait-Oufella H, Bige N, Boelle PY, et al. Capillary refill time exploration during septic shock. Intensive Care Med. 2014;40(7):958-964.
evidence.population: 59 consecutive adults with septic shock, tertiary ICU
evidence.quote: index CRT at 2.4 s predicted 14-day outcome with a sensitivity of 82% (95% CI [60-95]) and a specificity of 73% (95% CI [56-86])
evidence.target_condition: 14-day mortality after initial resuscitation of septic shock (index fingertip CRT >2.4 s at 6 h)

evidence.citation: Ait-Oufella H, Bige N, Boelle PY, et al. Capillary refill time exploration during septic shock. Intensive Care Med. 2014;40(7):958-964.
evidence.population: 59 consecutive adults with septic shock, tertiary ICU
evidence.quote: knee CRT at 4.9 s predicted 14-day outcome with a sensitivity of 82% (95% CI [60-95]) and a specificity of 84% (95% CI [68-94])
evidence.target_condition: 14-day mortality after initial resuscitation of septic shock (knee CRT >4.9 s at 6 h)

evidence.citation: Jacquet-Lagreze M, Wiart C, Schweizer R, et al. Prognostic value of capillary refill time in adult patients: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Crit Care. 2023;27(1):473.
evidence.population: Adults with acute circulatory failure; 13 studies in primary analysis (23 studies, 60,656 patients overall)
evidence.quote: pooled sensitivity was 54% (95%CI [43; 64]). The pooled specificity was 72% (95%CI [55; 84])
evidence.reference_standard: Mortality as reported by each study
evidence.target_condition: Death in adults with acute circulatory failure (abnormal CRT, study-specific thresholds)

examine.how: With the hand at heart level in a warm room, press the distal index finger pad (or nail bed) firmly for 10-15 s until blanched, release, and time return of baseline colour with a watch. Prolonged is >3 s (ICU studies use >2.4-3 s at the fingertip; knee CRT is an alternative site).
examine.negative_finding: A normal CRT does not exclude mild-to-moderate hypovolemia in adults (sensitivity 6% after 450 mL loss). In acute circulatory failure, normal CRT only weakly lowers mortality risk (pooled LR- about 0.6).
examine.pitfalls: Cold room, cold hands, age and vasoconstriction prolong CRT without hypoperfusion; measurement quality (site, pressure, timing) strongly affects accuracy. CRT is a prognostic/perfusion marker, not a diagnostic test for the cause of shock.
examine.positive_finding: In resuscitated septic shock, a fingertip CRT >2.4 s at 6 h predicts 14-day death with sensitivity 82% and specificity 73%, and marks persisting hypoperfusion. In undifferentiated adults, a prolonged CRT is a weak sign of hypovolemia (sensitivity 26-46%).
examine.prerequisites: Warm extremity and ambient temperature; a second hand or watch to time; consistent pressure (a glass slide can standardise blanching).
examine.title: Capillary refill time prolonged (>2-3 s, fingertip at heart level, warm room)

examine.changes_what: A dry axilla modestly raises the probability of hypovolemia and supports checking electrolytes, BUN/creatinine and giving a fluid trial; a moist axilla does not exclude it.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid if axillary skin is broken or infected.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use to exclude hemorrhage or shock; the RCE data apply to vomiting/diarrhea/poor intake, not blood loss.
examine.escalation_warning: Hypotension, severe postural dizziness or a postural pulse rise of 30/min or more indicates significant volume loss regardless of axillary moisture.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Adults (largely elderly) presenting with suspected hypovolemia due to vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake
evidence.quote: the presence of a dry axilla supports the diagnosis of hypovolemia (positive likelihood ratio, 2.8; 95% CI, 1.4-5.4)
evidence.reference_standard: Laboratory/clinical criteria for hypovolemia used by the included primary studies (e.g. serum osmolality, urea/creatinine); details not visible in abstract
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (dehydration) in adults with vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake

examine.how: With the patient supine or seated and the arm relaxed, place a dry, ungloved finger or the back of the hand into the axillary vault and feel for moisture. Check both axillae; the sign is positive when neither axilla is moist to touch.
examine.negative_finding: Moist axillae argue only weakly against hypovolemia; the negative LR was not reported in the RCE abstract and the sign has low sensitivity.
examine.pitfalls: Anticholinergic drugs, autonomic neuropathy, cold environments and antiperspirants dry the axilla without hypovolemia; sweating from fever or anxiety can mask true volume depletion.
examine.positive_finding: Both axillae dry to touch, supporting hypovolemia in a patient with vomiting, diarrhea or poor oral intake (LR+ about 2.8).
examine.prerequisites: Axilla not recently washed, dried or covered by antiperspirant; room not cold. Compare with the patient's baseline sweating if known.
examine.title: Dry axilla

examine.changes_what: Moist membranes and an unfurrowed tongue lower the probability of hypovolemia; dry findings support a fluid trial and checking electrolytes, BUN/creatinine.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not validated for blood loss; do not use these signs to exclude hemorrhagic hypovolemia or shock.
examine.escalation_warning: Hypotension, severe postural dizziness or a postural pulse increment of 30/min or more indicates large volume loss and needs urgent resuscitation regardless of mucosal findings.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Adults (largely elderly) presenting with suspected hypovolemia due to vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake
evidence.quote: moist mucous membranes and a tongue without furrows argue against it (negative likelihood ratio, 0.3; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6 for both findings)
evidence.reference_standard: Laboratory/clinical criteria for hypovolemia used by the included primary studies; details not visible in abstract
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (dehydration) in adults with vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake - finding: dry oral mucous membranes (LR- is for moist membranes)

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Adults (largely elderly) presenting with suspected hypovolemia due to vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake
evidence.quote: moist mucous membranes and a tongue without furrows argue against it (negative likelihood ratio, 0.3; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6 for both findings)
evidence.reference_standard: Laboratory/clinical criteria for hypovolemia used by the included primary studies; details not visible in abstract
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (dehydration) in adults with vomiting, diarrhea or decreased oral intake - finding: longitudinal tongue furrows (LR- is for tongue without furrows)

examine.how: Inspect the mouth with a light: look at the buccal mucosa and under the tongue for moisture, and at the dorsum of the tongue for longitudinal furrows. Inspect the eyes for sunken globes. Palpate the axilla for sweat. Record each sign separately rather than a global impression.
examine.negative_finding: Moist mucous membranes or a tongue without furrows argue against hypovolemia (LR- 0.3 for either), which is the more useful direction of these signs.
examine.pitfalls: Mouth breathing, oxygen therapy, anticholinergics and age-related changes dry the mouth without volume depletion; sunken eyes and tongue furrows are chronic in many elderly patients.
examine.positive_finding: Dry mucous membranes, furrowed tongue, sunken eyes or a dry axilla each support hypovolemia in patients with vomiting, diarrhea or poor intake; the pooled RCE gives LR+ 2.8 for dry axilla only.
examine.prerequisites: Patient not mouth-breathing on oxygen for a prolonged period and no recent oral intake or mouth care; good lighting.
examine.title: Dry oral mucous membranes, tongue furrows, sunken eyes, dry axilla
